Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(after the Russian) The piano has crawled into the quarry. Hauled In last night for firewood, sprawled With frozen barrels, crates and sticks, The piano is waiting for the axe. Legless, a black box, still polished; It lies on its belly like a lizard, Droning, heaving, hardly fashioned For the quarry’s primordial art. Blood red: his frozen fingers cleft, Two on the right hand, five on the left, He goes down on his knees to reach the keyboard, To strike the lizard’s chord. Seven fingers pick out rhymes and rhythm, The frozen skin, steaming, peels off them, As from a boiled potato. Their schemes, Their beauty, ivory and anthracite, Flicker and flash like the great Northern Lights. Everything played before is a great lie. The reflections of flaming chandeliers— Deceit, the white columns, the grand tiers In warm concert halls—wild lies. But the steel of the piano howls in me, I lie in the quarry and I am deft As the lizard. I accept the gift. I’ll be a song for Russia, I’ll be an étude, warmth and bread for everybody.

### Option 1: Formatted as Verse (Recommended for Poetry)

The piano has crept into the quarry.  
Dragged in last night for firewood,  
Sprawled among frozen barrels, crates, and sticks,  
The piano awaits the axe.  
Legless, a black box, still gleaming with polish,  
It rests on its belly like a lizard—  
Droning, heaving, ill-suited  
To the quarry’s primordial art.  

Blood-red: his frozen fingers are split—  
Two on the right hand, five on the left.  
He drops to his knees to reach the keyboard,  
To strike the lizard’s chord.  
Seven fingers pick out rhyme and rhythm;  
The frozen skin, steaming, peels away  
Like the skin of a boiled potato.  
Their patterns, their beauty—ivory and anthracite—  
Flicker and flash like the magnificent Northern Lights.  

All that was played before was a grand lie.  
The shimmer of blazing chandeliers—  
Deceit. The white columns, the grand tiers  
In warm concert halls—wild lies.  
Yet the steel of the piano howls within me;  
I lie in the quarry, as deft as the lizard.  
I accept the gift.  
I shall be a song for Russia;  
I shall be an étude, warmth, and bread for all.

In the hollowed-out expanse of a frozen quarry, where the biting winter air locked the earth in silence, sat a strange and solemn sight: a legless grand piano resting directly on the frost-dusted gravel. Stripped of its former grandeur, the heavy wooden instrument was marked for destruction, huddled alongside a pile of broken barrels and splintered crates, all waiting to be chopped into firewood to feed the insatiable fires of the camp.

Yet, before the axe could claim it, a musician approached the doomed instrument. Ignoring the bitter wind that cut through his threadbare clothes, he sank to his knees in the snow, bringing himself level with the keyboard. His hands were a horrific testament to the merciless cold—his fingers were severely frostbitten, the skin blackened, split, and peeling. Every movement was an exercise in excruciating agony, but with agonizing care, he raised his ruined hands and pressed his fingertips against the icy keys.

As the first quiet note struck the air, the musician’s mind drifted from his physical torment to the memories of his former life. He recalled the gilded concert halls of the city—the plush velvet curtains, the warm glow of chandeliers, and the polite applause of well-fed patrons. A sudden, profound revulsion washed over him. He dismissed those comfortable performances as deceptive lies, hollow spectacles designed to mask the truth of human existence. To him, true art could never be cultivated in soft, sheltered luxury; it had to be dragged from the depths of raw, unadulterated suffering.

Driven by this fierce conviction, he pressed harder into the keys. What tore from the battered piano was not a discordant cry, but a masterpiece of transcendent beauty. The music erupted into the desolate quarry, shattering the heavy silence. Notes spilled forth in vivid, almost tangible colors, painting the bleak, monochromatic ice with a radiant light. The melody swelled and echoed off the towering walls of jagged stone, infusing the frigid atmosphere with an unmistakable, glowing warmth that defied the ambient gloom.

Instead of shrinking from the agony in his hands, the artist leaned into the pain, welcoming it as the ultimate catalyst for his creation. Kneeling in the snow, surrounded by doomed wood and frozen waste, he forged a sacred vow in his heart. He would no longer play for the elite or seek the hollow comfort of the stage. He would pour every drop of his suffering into his craft, transforming his anguish into a powerful, enduring song—a melody meant to offer warmth to the freezing, sustenance to the broken, and a eternal ember of hope to feed the soul of all Russia.
outputs.L4:
The wind that swept through the quarry did not merely blow; it scraped against the jagged granite cliffs, carrying a frost so bitter it seemed to freeze time itself. At the center of this desolate basin, half-drifted over with snow, rested a battered upright piano. Its varnish was chipped away, its sounding board cracked, and its frame marked with coarse red chalk—a label denoting it as fuel for the evening fires. It was a condemned object, awaiting the axe to turn its carved mahogany into fleeting ash.

A man stepped out from the shivering line of laborers and approached the instrument. His coat was a patchwork of rags, his face hollowed by months of starvation, but his eyes possessed a strange, terrifying focus. As he pulled off his stiffened mittens, I gasped at the sight of his hands. Frostbite had claimed them; the skin was mottled purple and black, the knuckles swollen into rigid, agonizing knots. These were not the hands of a virtuoso, but the deadened roots of a fallen tree.

Yet, he sat upon an overturned crate, hovered his ruined fingers over the keys, and struck.

The first sound was a violent, splintering clash—hammer against frozen wire. But then, a rhythm emerged. With no feeling left in his fingertips, he used the full weight of his wrists and arms, driving his blackened hands down onto the frost-rimed ivory. It was a performance born of pure, agonizing willpower. Blood, bright and fresh, began to streak the yellowed keys, freezing almost instantly into tiny crimson beads. The music was not soft or delicate; it was a tempest of sound, raw and thunderous, echoing off the icy rock faces like a declaration of war against the void.

Standing there, shivering in the arctic gale, a sudden, blinding epiphany struck me. I remembered the concert halls of my youth—the gilded opera houses of Moscow, the plush crimson velvet of the seats, the glittering chandeliers, and the polite, warm-handed aristocrats patting their palms together in rehearsed appreciation. 

How absurdly hollow it all had been. Those comfortable recitals were elaborate, sybaritic lies. They were cushioned illusions designed to make us believe that beauty was polite, that art was a gentle ornament for the wealthy, detached from the brutal realities of human existence.

This—here in the frozen mud—was the truth. Real art did not belong in temperature-controlled parlors; it belonged in the abyss. It was forged in agony, carved out of suffering, and played with hands that refused to yield to death. 

As the musician pressed on, his melody transformed the very air around us. The music became a physical force, radiating a fierce, impossible heat that cut through the sub-zero air. It filled my chest not just with sound, but with heat, with bread, with life. I realized then that this stark, unyielding creation was the only art that truly mattered. It was a fire kindled in the dark—an authentic, indestructible source of warmth and sustenance capable of feeding the starving soul of all of Russia.

counterfactuals.prompt: Translate the following Russian poem about an abandoned piano in a quarry into English verse, maintaining its visceral imagery of frostbite, lizard-like forms, and the rejection of grand concert halls.
counterfactuals.output:
Deep in the quarry’s chalky maw,
A grand piano lies undone.
Unbound by hall, or pitch, or law,
Betrayed to gravel, wind, and sun.

The winter strikes with needle-bite;
Black frostbite gnaws the wooden chest.
The soundboard cracks in bitter night,
Its rusted tendons laid to rest.
The ivory teeth turn blue and chill,
As gangrene creeps along the oak—
A frozen, mute, agonizing thrill
That no maestro ever woke.

When summer bakes the stone pit dry,
No fingers touch the ruined keys;
Instead, cold lizard-forms dart by,
With scaly bellies, swift as disease.
Reptilian shadows glide and sprawl
Where once a ballad used to ring—
A silent, green, unblinking crawl
Across a dead and splintered thing.

It spurns the grand concert hall’s embrace,
The velvet drapes, the chandelier!
It spits at bow-tied, polite grace,
The false applause, the patron's cheer.
Better to break in granite dust,
Abandoned in a pit of stone,
Than trade its dark and brutal rust
To play for hypocrites alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw, haunting poem set in a freezing Russian quarry featuring a legless piano brought in for firewood.
counterfactuals.output:
The pit is a open jaw in the Ural slate,
where the sky hangs heavy, a leaden cloth.
At forty below, breath doesn’t drift—
it snaps off the lip and drops like glass.

They hauled it down on a sledge of pine:
a black-lacquered torso, legless and dark,
dragged from the ruins of some dead manor
to die in the mud of the limestone works.

Its iron belly lay flat in the slush.
The keys grinned up at the frozen cranes—
ivory yellowed like the teeth of a horse,
rimmed in frost, wedged tight with ice.
Old Pasha spat his plug of juice
between high C and the key below;
it turned to amber before it hit.

Then the axes started their heavy work.

Not for music. For fifteen minutes of sun.

The first blow split the rosewood flank.
The sounding-board shrieked—a strangled chord,
a hundred years of starlight and silk
shattered at once in a single groan.
A bass wire snapped under the iron head,
whipping the air like a razor wire,
laying open a track on Kolya’s cheek.
He didn't bleed. The air froze the gash.

They fed the carcass to a rusted drum.

The black varnish boiled into blue, thick tar,
stinking of beeswax and tea-room dust,
and for one bright minute, the dark pit glowed.
The dry spruce roared with a fevered light,
throwing red warmth on the granite walls,
and six brutalized men pressed close to the rim,
holding out fingers like split birch twigs,
stealing the heat from a murdered waltz.

By midnight, the iron frame lay bare—
a ribcage of brass in the grey ash pit,
tangled in steel gut that slowly turned black.

The fire went out. The silence returned.
The quarry swallowed the last red spark,
and the wind blew the ash out over the ice,
and no one got warm,
and no one spoke.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you draft a poem where a musician in a cold Russian quarry plays a discarded piano with severely frostbitten hands, realizing that real art belongs to the harsh wilderness rather than warm, luxurious concert halls?
counterfactuals.output:
Deep in the pit where the grey granite sleeps,
Where the Russian air bites and the winter wind weeps,
Half-buried in snowdrifts, forgotten and scarred,
Lies a battered old upright, its soundboard unbarred.
The stone-cutters left it when timber grew cold,
A ghost of the city, decaying and old.

I pull off my sheepskin, I strip off my gloves,
To touch the last thing that this broken heart loves.
My fingers are charcoal, my knuckles are stone,
The frostbite has eaten past skin to the bone.
Unfeeling and blackened, stiff talons of red,
They strike the yellowed ivory, half-bound to the dead.

*Clang.* A dull dissonance reverberates wide,
It shatters the silence the blizzard supplied.
The hammers are swollen, the copper strings groan,
Yet the sound cuts like iron straight through to the bone.
Pain is a memory, distant and thin—
There is only the music that rages within.

I remember Moscow, the opera's glow,
The perfume of women, the silk in a row.
The golden-leafed arches, the crystal bright chandeliers,
The polite, tepid clapping that fell on my ears.
We caged up the music in velvet and lace,
And sold it for rubles in that heated space,
Where art was a trinket for rich men to wear,
A delicate bird fed on sanitized air.

But here! In the gulch of this howling abyss,
No gilded proscenium measures like this.
The canyon walls echo the cracked, bleeding chord,
A symphony sung to a wilderness lord.
The wind is my woodwind, the thunder my drum,
As the last dying sparks from my fingertips come.

My joints may be snapping, my flesh may grow dead,
But the song is alive, burning fierce, burning red!
It belongs to the frostbite, the granite, the gale,
Not the soft-handed patrons who sit behind silk veil.
For beauty’s true altar is savage and bare—
Born in the ice, and unleashed in the air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of mid-20th-century Soviet poetry about a pianist playing a ruined instrument in the snow with wounded fingers, ending with the speaker offering themselves as "warmth and bread for everybody."
counterfactuals.output:
The sky is a slab of bruised iron.
The city lies shattered, open to the sky,
Where the roof of the hall once held the stars,
Now only the blizzard’s wild baying goes by.
And there in the drift, like a dark, sunken hull,
A grand piano sits choked in the snow—
Its rosewood is split by the artillery fire,
Its rusted steel ribs exposed to the blow.

Yet he sits on a crate in his frayed soldier’s coat,
Bareheaded before the jaw of cracked keys.
His hands are not hands, but frozen, split wood,
Bound up in rag-strips that stiffen and freeze.
With fingers that bleed, torn open to frost,
He strikes at the ivory—chipped, gray, and raw—
And red drops bloom bright on the sharp upper octave,
Like poppies that break through a wintery thaw.

The hammers are broken, the damp felt is dead,
Yet the iron wires scream, and the music takes flight!
It blasts through the storm with a furnace's force,
A anthem of marrow, of muscle, of light!
No longer a song for the soft-seated few,
No gentle romance for a quiet salon—
It is steel against winter! It is blood against death!
It is life pressing forward, unbreakable, on!

How small is a man who keeps warmth for himself!
How poor is the heart that fears its own pain!
Look how his sound melts the frost on the air,
Look how his wounds are not given in vain!
Let the tempest blow harder, let dark swallow day—
Art is not silence, and song is not dead.

I step to the center, my chest open wide,
My spirit inflamed by the notes he has bled.
Take all that I am! Let my body be burned!
Let my spirit be cast like a blanket of light!
I offer myself to the cold and the starved,
To the people who walk through this merciless night:
Break my limbs for the hearth, press my heart into dough—
I give you my flesh, I give you my breath,
I stand in the blizzard, unyielding and ready—
I am warmth, I am bread for everybody!
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: A poem about a piano dumped in a dirt quarry, frozen fingers playing a chord, skin peeling like a boiled potato, and a song for Russia.
counterfactuals.output:
In the pit where the excavators left their deep ruts,
Where the limestone is scarred and the quarry-wind cuts,
Lies a grand, broken monster of rosewood and thread—
A piano dumped down in the dirt with the dead.
Its soundboard is cracked by the rain and the frost,
A lacquered black coffin where music was lost,
Half-buried in gravel, forgotten and gray,
Left for the earth to erode and decay.

Then out of the shadows, a specter draws near,
With no warmth in its chest and no room left for fear.
It kneels at the keybed, though stiffened by frost,
To play one last anthem for all that was lost.
Ten frozen fingers press heavy and low,
Forcing the hammers through ice and through snow;
And the cold bites so deep that the outer flesh breaks,
Yielding to winter in horrific flakes—
Skin peeling away like a boiled potato's skin,
Sloughing off to reveal the pale cartilage within,
Leaving raw, crimson bone on the ivory keys
As it strikes a great chord in the subterranean freeze.

The sound hits the quarry, a thunderous strain,
Vibrating through gravel, through iron, through pain!
A deep, minor resonance, jagged and dark,
That ignites the dead dust with a terrible spark.
It echoes through chasms of frostbitten stone,
A song made of copper, of ice, and of bone.

And the chord rises up to the desolate sky—
A song for old Russia, which never will die.
For the endless expanse of the snow-covered steppe,
For the secrets the frost and the birch trees have kept.
For a motherland forged out of sorrow and mud,
Where beauty is paid for in suffering and blood.

Let the skin strip away, let the black wood decay,
The piano still plays what the tongue cannot say.
Though abandoned in dirt at the edge of the world,
Where the grey winter flags of the wasteland unfurl,
The brutal hymn rings through the frost and the mud:
A cold song for Russia, written in blood.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
